concept: deixis
statement: Deictic expressions are interpreted relative to utterance-act roles, time or place, normally from the speaker/writer's perspective but sometimes from a shifted centre such as the reader of a public notice or a person whose thoughts are reported.
condition: Identify utterance-anchored person, temporal and locative reference (I, you, now, yesterday, here, this, that), while permitting contextually shifted reader-centred and reported-perspective interpretations rather than requiring every example to use the speaker's immediate time and place.

exceptions.description: The deictic centre may shift to the current reader of a notice or to a reported person's perspective rather than the speaker/writer's own time.

correct.text: I'll see you here tomorrow.
Look at that.
We left yesterday.
I will return next week. [I and next week anchored to the speaker]
[Public notice] Now show your pass. [now can refer to the reader's time]

concept: anaphora and pro-forms
statement: Anaphora is the relation between an anaphor and its antecedent: the anaphor's interpretation derives from the antecedent; anaphors may be personal pronouns and other pro-forms (so, do so, one) or gaps, and the relation can be shown by co-indexing.
condition: Applies to expressions interpreted by reference to an antecedent: pronouns, pro-forms such as so, do so and one, and gaps in elliptical clauses.

correct.text: Jill has left her car in the road. [her = Jill]
Grapes are expensive and likely to remain so. [so]
I haven't told them yet, but I'll do so tomorrow. [do so]
This banana is green: have you got a riper one? [one]
I'd like to help you but I can't. [gap]

concept: order of anaphor and antecedent
statement: An anaphor generally follows its antecedent, but under restricted conditions it may precede it.
condition: Applies to anaphors and antecedents: the default order is antecedent first; the conditions allowing the reverse are not spelled out in this overview.

correct.text: Jill has left her car in the road.

contrast.text: If you can, please come a little earlier next week.
contrast.note: Anaphor (gap after can) precedes its antecedent (come earlier).

concept: utterance-act anchoring of deictic reference
statement: Deictic reference shifts systematically with the time, place or participants of an utterance-act; a proper name may vary in reference without having such a deictic meaning.
condition: When interpreting I, now, here, this or that, identify the relevant utterance-act anchor; contrast with a proper name whose choice of bearer is context-dependent but not systematically anchored to utterance roles.

contrast.text: A says, 'I will call tomorrow.' [I refers to A]
B says, 'I will call tomorrow.' [I refers to B]
A says, 'Casey called.' [the proper name is not deictic]
B says, 'Casey called.' [a different Casey may be intended]

concept: deictic and non-deictic spatial and temporal location
statement: Time and place may be located deictically relative to an utterance-act or non-deictically relative to a named place or independently identified event.

concept: deictic expression versus deictic marker
statement: A deictic expression is the whole utterance-anchored referring constituent; its deictic marker is the word that encodes this property, which may be a proper part of the expression or the entire expression.
condition: In those blue folders, treat the NP as the expression and those as its marker; in last month, last is the marker; with a stand-alone item such as here, marker and expression coincide.

concept: indexing acts in deictic interpretation
statement: Pointing, gaze, touch and diagrammatic marks can identify deictic referents and cooperate with nominal descriptions; gestures are sometimes necessary but are not universally required.

concept: speaker-centred deictic centre
statement: The deictic centre is ordinarily the speaker or writer and changes between speakers; expressions written in a personal message may be anchored to the time of writing rather than reading.
condition: Interpret first-person, local and temporal deictics by default from the current utterer's perspective and recalculate that anchor after a conversational speaker change, subject to specially shifted-centre uses.

exceptions.description: Deictic interpretation can shift from the speaker/writer to a reader of a standing notice or a represented thinker's viewpoint, as the same subsection expressly notes.

[Notice] 'Now submit your ticket.' [now shifts to each reader's time rather than the writer's]

concept: reader-centred deixis in standing written notices

concept: punctuation indicators
statement: Punctuation indicators are written devices that give cues to grammatical structure or meaning, including marks, spaces and eligible changes of typography.
condition: For a stretch of written text, identify a punctuation indicator by the grammatical or interpretive cue it supplies, not simply by whether it is a separate printed symbol.

contrast.text: The note ends 'The lane is clear.' [full stop is an indicator]
A sentence starts 'Tomorrow we leave.' [initial capital is an indicator]
The invented novel title Winter Harbour is printed in italics. [type style marks a title]
The phrase 'Well, we tried' contains a comma. [structural cue]

concept: segmental punctuation indicators
statement: Segmental punctuation indicators take up distinct positions in written linear sequences; the category comprises punctuation marks and word spaces.
condition: Identify a written mark or word-separating blank as segmental when it occupies an independent place in the string, as opposed to changing the presentation of a letter.

contrast.text: Rain fell, then stopped. [comma is a segmental mark]

Is the bridge open? [terminal question mark]

concept: non-segmental punctuation modifications
statement: Non-segmental punctuation modifies existing written symbols through features such as capitalisation, italics, bold face or small capitals when they serve a punctuation-related purpose.
condition: When a change of case or type style conveys sentence beginning, quotation, title or emphasis, classify the change as a non-segmental punctuation modification rather than as another written segment.

exceptions.description: Type styling used solely to show larger heading or chapter hierarchy is outside this definition of punctuation.

concept: sentence-opening and sentence-closing indicators
statement: In ordinary writing sentence beginnings are indicated non-segmentally through an initial capital, while sentence endings are marked segmentally by a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.

concept: word-internal punctuation marks
statement: Apostrophes and hyphens are punctuation marks normally placed within orthographic words, unlike most marks delimiting expressions or sentences.

concept: diacritics as spelling rather than punctuation
statement: Diacritics on letters are normally aspects of word spelling rather than punctuation, although a diaeresis can have a borderline hyphen-like function in certain American spellings.
condition: For accents and other diacritics in a word, treat them as word-spelling rather than punctuational indicators, except for the borderline use of a diaeresis to mark a vowel break in some AmE forms.

concept: punctuation beyond the single sentence
statement: Punctuation may operate above sentence level: quotation marks and parentheses can enclose several sentences, and paragraph breaks may be indicated by a new line and usually indentation.

concept: Primary tense, secondary tense, aspect and mood as distinct systems
statement: English verbal grammar distinguishes primary tense, secondary tense, progressive aspect and modal mood as four formally separable systems.
condition: Classify a verbal construction by its present/preterite morphology, perfect have, progressive be and modal auxiliary pattern.

correct.text: The employees have been working. [perfect and progressive]

concept: Progressive aspect presents an internal temporal view
statement: Progressive aspect views a situation from within its unfolding rather than locating it in a different primary tense.
condition: A clause contrasts progressive be plus gerund-participle with the corresponding non-progressive form at the same primary tense.

correct.text: The gardeners were planting trees.

concept: Temporal-location adjuncts differ for states and non-progressive events
statement: A temporal-location adjunct can fall inside a state's duration, while with a non-progressive occurrence it typically locates the occurrence as a whole.
condition: A temporal adjunct occurs with a stative clause, a non-progressive occurrence or a progressive occurrence.

correct.text: At noon, the students were still in the library. [state]
At noon, the students were preparing the presentation. [progressive event]

concept: Eventive pseudo-clefts with do
statement: Pseudo-cleft constructions with what someone did normally predicate an occurrence, not an unchanging state.
condition: A pseudo-cleft headed by what an agent did is followed by a verb expression describing an action or dynamic event.

concept: Achievements are punctual; processes durative
statement: Achievements are conceptualised as punctual transitions, while processes unfold over a duration.
condition: A situation is classified as an achievement or process by whether its central development is instantaneous or extended.

correct.text: The visitor located the exit. [achievement]
The visitor searched the building. [process]

concept: Accomplishment telicity versus activity atelicity
statement: Accomplishments are durative events with a natural completion point, whereas activities do not inherently reach a defined terminal result.
condition: A dynamic process includes or excludes a specified bounded endpoint.

correct.text: Lina painted a particular wall. [accomplishment]
Lina painted walls for a living. [activity]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No verified Burton-Roberts source mapping for this passage.

concept: Bounded objects can determine lexical telicity
statement: A bounded object or destination can convert an activity-type predicate into an accomplishment with an inherent endpoint.
condition: An action such as read, write or walk receives an object/distance complement that bounds the event.

correct.text: They walked to the lighthouse. [telic]
They walked along the beach. [atelic]

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Bounded objects can determine lexical telicity

concept: Accomplishments contain pre-terminal and terminal phases
statement: An accomplishment has a durative pre-terminal development and a punctual terminal phase, unlike an unbounded activity or a single achievement.
condition: An event has a specified result reached only after a process unfolds.

correct.text: The crew built a shelter. [accomplishment]
The child skipped for an hour. [activity]

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Accomplishments contain pre-terminal and terminal phases

concept: Aspectual verbs with punctual achievements
statement: Begin, stop and related lexical aspectual predicates generally select processes rather than single punctual achievements, but repeated achievements can be licensed.
condition: A punctual achievement predicate is embedded under an aspectual lexical verb with a singular or repeated-event interpretation.

correct.text: The team began repairing the roof. [process]
The athlete kept reaching the finish line first. [repeated achievements]

concept: Finish versus stop with accomplishments
statement: Finishing an accomplishment entails completion of its endpoint, while stopping it merely ends the ongoing activity without necessarily completing the result.
condition: A process with a built-in endpoint is embedded under finish or stop.

correct.text: They finished restoring the mural. [completed]
They stopped restoring the mural. [may be incomplete]

concept: Strict versus extendable achievements in progressive aspect
statement: Strict achievements tend to resist the progressive, whereas extendable achievements such as dying can receive a durative progressive interpretation.
condition: A punctual event predicate is used with progressive be and must be classified for whether a transitional process is available.

correct.text: The patient was dying when we arrived. [extendable achievement]
The scientist noticed the irregularity. [strict achievement]

statement: A progressive activity entails that some activity took place, but a progressive accomplishment does not entail reaching its terminal result.
condition: A progressive clause describes an atelic activity versus a telic accomplishment, with different implications about completion.

correct.text: The children were playing, so they played. [activity]
Mina was composing an essay, but she never finished it. [accomplishment]

condition: A temporal-duration adjunct modifies an activity, accomplishment or achievement, including the preceding or resulting state rather than the event itself.

concept: Iterative, repeated, and serial situation multiplicity

condition: The source describes more than one occurrence of a situation, with the subsituations characterised by lexical event meaning, count, or habit.

condition: An iterative or habitual predicate is interpreted at both the single-occurrence and overall-series levels.

concept: Iterative punctual events as activity
statement: Repeated punctual achievements can together form an activity compatible with progressives and duration adjuncts.
condition: A lexical event such as knocking, nodding or blinking may be interpreted as a succession of very brief individual events.

statement: Serial habitual situations are stative overall even when the repeated subsituations are dynamic.
condition: A predicate expresses habitual recurrence, potentially using an overt frequency adverb or an understood routine.

correct.text: She usually swims before breakfast.

concept: Perfective and imperfective aspectuality as interpretations
statement: Perfective aspectuality presents a situation as a whole, while imperfective aspectuality presents an internal temporal perspective.
condition: Classify the interpretation of a situation according to whether it is taken as complete overall or viewed within an ongoing state or event.

correct.text: The author finished the manuscript last Friday. [perfective]
The author was writing the manuscript then. [imperfective]

concept: Progressive aspect as a form of imperfective viewpoint
statement: The English be-plus-gerund-participle construction conventionally expresses an ongoing dynamic situation and therefore a progressive type of imperfectivity.
condition: Classify the aspectual meaning of be followed by the verbal gerund-participle, when that be is progressive auxiliary rather than passive or copular.

correct.text: She is preparing the slides.
They were walking toward the venue.

concept: Simple present habitual states contrasted with perfective occurrences
statement: A non-progressive clause may have a perfective interpretation for a single dynamic occurrence but an imperfective interpretation for a habitual series.
condition: Identify whether a finite verb describes one bounded dynamic event or a recurring practice rather than treating the simple-form morphology as a universal aspect marker.

correct.text: He planted a tree yesterday. [single occurrence]
He planted a tree every spring. [past habitual series]

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No independently verified Burton-Roberts crosswalk is claimed.

review_notes: Source-checked against printed pages of the supplied Cambridge PDF; examples are newly authored. This is explanatory classification, not a blanket error prohibition. A habitual preterite does not necessarily assert that the entire habitual state ended in the past.

concept: Primary tense and temporal relation model
statement: Primary tense relates a referred time to an orientation time: anterior for past, simultaneous for present, and posterior for future.
condition: Analyse a tensed clause with respect to reference time Tr and orientation time To, distinguishing the relation from the verb's exact event duration.

correct.text: She left before noon. [anterior]
She works here now. [simultaneous reference]
When she visits tomorrow, we will talk. [posterior]

concept: Reference time and situation time distinguished
statement: With perfective interpretation the reference time may coincide with the whole event, while in imperfective interpretation it may identify only part of a longer situation.
condition: Distinguish Tr, the time used for tense interpretation, from Tsit, the interval over which the state or event obtains.

correct.text: The bridge collapsed at dawn. [reference tracks the event]

concept: Deictic time in recorded and written utterances
statement: Deictic time may be anchored to the production of an utterance or, in notices and recorded communications, to when an addressee encounters it.
condition: Interpret present and past reference in speech, letters, posted notices and similar delayed-message settings.

correct.text: I am typing this message now. [production time]

concept: Non-deictic orientation time in embedded tense
statement: A tense in an embedded clause can be interpreted relative to a contextual orientation time rather than the speech time.
condition: A complement reports what somebody might later say or think, or otherwise establishes a perspective internal to a future or past situation.

correct.text: If she wins, she will say she trained well.

concept: Four temporal notions Tr, To, Tsit and Td
statement: Temporal analysis distinguishes reference time, orientation time, situation time and deictic time rather than treating all four as one instant.
condition: Represent a clause's tense and aspect interpretation, allowing Tr to be internal to Tsit and To to differ from Td.

concept: Simple present for states and performatives
statement: Ordinary simple-present statives cover an interval containing the reference time, while performative utterances can make a bounded event coincide with the act of saying it.
condition: A finite simple present verb expresses a state obtaining at the present orientation time or a conventional speech act accomplished through its utterance.

correct.text: I own a bicycle. [state]

concept: Limited and unlimited states in simple present
statement: The same simple-present construction can describe temporary states, enduring states and general truths.
condition: Determine the temporal duration of an ordinary state from lexical and contextual information, not from a separate present-tense inflection.

correct.text: She has a cold this week.
The chemical formula remains unchanged under these conditions.

concept: Habitual reading of extended dynamic simple present
statement: A dynamic predicate requiring longer than a speech act generally receives a habitual or serial-state reading in the simple present.
condition: A speaker uses an ordinary simple-present accomplishment or activity without a commentary, performative or special narrative context.

correct.text: I solve crossword puzzles on weekends.
My neighbour builds model boats.

concept: Running commentary and demonstrations in simple present
statement: Simple-present dynamic predicates can report events as they unfold in conventional commentary or demonstrations.
condition: The speaker narrates a sequence of actions for an audience, possibly presenting a longer event as coextensive with the act of description.

correct.text: The runner reaches the finish line and celebrates.

burton_roberts_mapping.note: No independently verified Burton-Roberts crosswalk is claimed.

concept: Locative-present commentary formulae
statement: Short locative-first commentary clauses can use simple present for an ongoing event, often with a postposed non-pronominal subject.
condition: A semi-formulaic sequence begins with here, there, up or down and describes a salient immediate motion or arrival.

correct.text: Here comes the bus.
There goes the last train.

concept: Timeless present in synopses and stage directions
statement: Simple present can describe the contents of narratives or stage directions without locating their events at the present time of speaking.
condition: A clause summarises the actions of fictional characters or specifies staged action as part of a reusable script.

correct.text: In the opening scene, the detective discovers the hidden letter.
The actor moves toward the window. [stage direction]

concept: Present reference to enduring texts and artworks
statement: Present tense can describe what an enduring text or artwork depicts or says, even though it was created in the past.

concept: Present tense in captions, chronicles and historic narrative
statement: Captions, historical chronologies and vivid conversational narratives may use present tense to depict events that occurred in the past.

concept: Recent-past newspaper headline present
statement: News headlines can use simple present to report events in the recent past, while the accompanying article uses past or present perfect tense.
condition: A news headline refers to a recently completed event and adopts vivid, compact headline style.

concept: Present futurate in a main clause
statement: Simple present in a main clause can locate a situation in the future when the situation is determined by conditions already known now.
condition: A main clause describes a cyclic natural event, a currently scheduled occurrence, or a predetermined consequence of a condition.

concept: Cyclic natural events licensing futurate present

concept: Scheduled versus predicted future event
statement: A scheduled future activity may take simple present, while an unscheduled prediction of its outcome typically takes modal will or another future expression.
condition: The speaker distinguishes a current arrangement from a hoped-for or predicted result whose outcome is not already settled.

concept: Conditional futurate and predetermined consequence
statement: Simple present can express a future consequence treated as inevitable or already decided when a condition is met.

concept: Present versus past anchor of a futurate
statement: The future event time and the time at which a schedule is known are separable, allowing present and preterite futurates to describe the same event from different reference points.
condition: A schedule now or at some earlier time determines an event that lies later than the scheduling time.

correct.text: The exhibition opens next Monday. [current schedule]
At the time, the exhibition opened the following Monday. [past schedule]

concept: Two temporal adjuncts in one futurate clause
statement: A futurate clause can carry a temporal expression for the time of an arrangement and a distinct expression for the future event.
condition: A present- or past-anchored scheduling construction contains both an arrangement-time modifier and an event-time modifier.

correct.text: The concert now starts next Friday.
At that stage the race started on Sunday.

concept: Present versus non-past grammatical tense terminology
statement: The present tense remains a distinct primary tense category even though some subordinate clauses allow unrestricted future-time readings.
condition: A rule or lesson names the English tense contrasted with the preterite.

correct.text: The parcels arrive every morning. [present]
The parcels arrived yesterday. [preterite]

concept: Future-time simple present in subordinate non-assertive environments
statement: Certain subordinate clauses freely use simple present for future situations without requiring those situations to be currently scheduled or known.
condition: A subordinate temporal, conditional, relative, interrogative or related clause does not itself make an independent assertion that its future event will happen.

correct.text: We will begin when the speaker arrives.
If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.

sources.section: §4.2.5 Deictic future time in subordinate clauses

burton_roberts_mapping.br_concept: Future-time simple present in subordinate non-assertive environments

concept: Temporal subordinate clauses with future present
statement: Present tense in future-oriented temporal adjunct clauses can follow markers such as before, after, once, as soon as and when.
condition: The subordinate proposition is temporally linked to another event and may occur in future time.

correct.text: We will leave once the meeting ends.
I will call you before the train departs.

concept: Conditional and exhaustive condition future present
statement: Present tense can refer to future conditions under if, unless, provided, suppose and exhaustive whether constructions.
condition: A conditional protasis or exhaustive-condition clause presents a potential future condition without asserting its occurrence.

correct.text: We will stay if the guests arrive.
The result stands whether the witnesses agree or not.

concept: Future-oriented integrated relative and embedded interrogative clauses
statement: Integrated relative clauses and embedded interrogatives may use present tense for situations whose identity or answer will become available later.
condition: A restrictive relative or dependent interrogative has an unresolved future referent or value.

correct.text: Anyone who submits the form tomorrow will receive an email.
Tell me who wins the next round.

concept: Comparative clauses with present or future reading
statement: Comparative subordinate clauses can have either a present or future interpretation of a simple-present verb.
condition: A comparative construction relates a future event to another event whose timing may be present or future.

correct.text: Next month I will work faster than he works.
You should respond as she requests at the next meeting.

concept: Future present in complements of bet, hope and covert mandatives
statement: Some complements of betting and hoping predicates, and covert mandative clauses, permit simple present with future meaning.
condition: A subordinate content clause follows a licensing predicate or a mandative construction with a future situation.

correct.text: I hope she finishes the report tomorrow.
It is essential that he arrives prepared next week.

concept: Two temporal sources of future-present reference
statement: A subordinate future-present interpretation can arise either from reference posterior to a present orientation or from simultaneity with an already future orientation.
condition: A subordinate clause's tense must be interpreted with respect to its own deictic or non-deictic orientation time.

correct.text: We will wait until she returns. [posterior to present orientation]
She will say she feels better. [simultaneous with future reporting time]

concept: Anterior preterite for states and occurrences
statement: A preterite can present a past occurrence as a whole or locate a reference point within a state that may continue beyond that point.
condition: The preterite has a past orientation, and the predicate is interpreted either perfectively or imperfectively.

correct.text: The bridge collapsed during the storm.
I knew the answer at that moment.

concept: Politeness implicature with past-form predicates
statement: Past forms of wanting, hoping and wondering can convey politeness or diffidence without abandoning their ordinary past-time meaning.
condition: An interlocutor makes a request using a state predicate in the preterite or past progressive, often with a first-person subject.

correct.text: I wanted to ask a question.
I was hoping you could review my proposal.

concept: Preterite futurate relative to a past schedule
statement: A preterite or past progressive can describe a future event that had been scheduled relative to an earlier past orientation.
condition: A prior plan or arrangement established the later event, whether or not that event is future relative to the current utterance.

correct.text: At the time I was travelling the next day.
Originally, entries closed the following Friday.
